I'm not much of the traditional farmer people think about - though I do help out on one, but that's just for fun.

I grow, hunt, harvest, process, preserve, forage, and fish for much of my food stuffs. This is a choice, I could drive to the grocery store (though it's a bit of a drive) and save quite a bit of effort.
Do I want to know what unconventional meat is?

Venison, moose, bear, rabbit, wild turkey, duck, partridge, brook trout, brown trout, Atlantic salmon, and I get chicken, eggs, turkey, beef, and pork from the neighboring farm.

Cook it thoroughly and don't hunt for bears where the bears are unhealthy. In other words, don't hunt for bear near where people live. Those bears are probably eating trash and not the very healthiest to eat.

These are Maine black bears - ursa americana.
I've read that skinning and butchering black bears asap helps cut down on the game/grease flavor, unlike deer where you want to hang it up a couple days. I haven't had the chance to try it yet.

Skin and process as quickly as you can. Serve bear piping hot. If you let it cool down, even a little, it will have congealed fatty parts and not taste nearly as good.

I only harvest a bear every other year. So, I won't take one next year - as I'll still have some left. The following year, I'm going to take one during the archery season.

I grand slammed this year - Bear, Turkey, Whitetail, and Moose. It was my first attempt at grand slamming, but I'd hunted them all successfully before.
Gamey / greasiness comes from poor butchering. Bear fat is super oily. Remove it before butchering your meat. Render bear fat and use for making biscuits / pie crusts / soap etc

Trichinosis is the same thing that pork always had until very recently, which is why weve always cooked pork thoroughly. Besr and cougar carry trichinosis, but its no big deal. Just cook it all the way, and preferrably freeze it for a few months before cooking.

The average acre produces ~5000 pounds of blueberries (these are wild Maine blueberries) and the fields are harvested every other year - so 200 acres is harvested every year. On the year the field isn't harvested, it's the year we put hay down over it and burned it in the spring.

Is that the best way to re-nutritionalize the soil? Or inexpensive?

I always wondered how farmers tackled the obstacle of soil richness. In the Bible it commands people to let land lie fallow every seven years, I believe. Your method sounds better.

It kills the pests and unwanted vegetation. The berries grow back quicker as they prefer shallow soil atop ledge and slightly acidic soil. It's expensive because it means you can only harvest half the acreage per year. Fields are still sprayed, except the certified organic fields.
Is profit higher on organic or inorganic produce?

The profit is higher for organic but the market is smaller. Most of my berries go the Allen's where there's a cannery, the rest get sold directly or to a couple of smaller commercial outfits. They aren't separated from different growers, but if you Google Stonewall Kitchens, you can see one such company and order wild Maine blueberry products that have a moderate chance of having been sourced from my fields. Some go to make wine. The organics go to specific customers and get sold to a few local grocery stores and are also bought and resold at farmer's markets and health food stores.

These aren't commercial cultivars. They are low-bush and raked by hand. At that time of the year, I'll hire anyone with a pulse and a willingness to work. It's very hard work but it can be lucrative. Good rakers can earn $200+ in a day.
